analysis.one_liner: Bans doctors from sending patients to health businesses they or their families profit from.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the Senate, and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned doctors from referring patients to labs, imaging centers, equipment suppliers, and other health businesses in which the doctor or an immediate family member owned a stake or received payments, with exceptions for services done inside the doctor's own practice, rural providers, surgery centers, and hospital ownership above a set threshold. It would also have barred patients and insurers from being billed for services provided through a banned referral, required disclosure of physician owners, and imposed fines, lab certification suspensions, and Medicare exclusion for violators. It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, who would no longer face treatment decisions shaped by their doctor's own investments, and who could sue to recover payments for services provided through a banned referral; Medicare and private health insurers, which could refuse to pay claims arising from prohibited referrals; and independent testing labs, which would no longer compete against doctors' own facilities.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a physician from referring a patient to any health entity in which the physician or an immediate family member has an ownership or investment interest or a compensation arrangement, so a doctor's advice would not steer patients toward businesses the doctor profits from [S3].

Bars any claim, bill, or demand for payment for services furnished through a prohibited referral, meaning patients and third-party payors could not be forced to pay for them, and gives any person who paid such a claim the right to sue for a refund plus attorney's fees [S3].

Requires each health entity to disclose its ownership arrangements and the names of physicians with ownership stakes, and requires every bill to identify the referring physician, so payors could see who was referring [S3].

Imposes escalating sanctions for violations: civil fines up to $15,000 per referral (and up to $100,000 for cross-referral schemes), suspension or revocation of a referring laboratory's certification, and exclusion from Medicare and other federal health programs [S3].

Restricts ancillary providers such as diagnostic labs and imaging centers from billing anyone other than the patient or the payor the patient designated, curbing charges passed along without the patient's knowledge [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Physician-investors in clinical labs, imaging centers, medical equipment, and physical therapy businesses, who would lose the income stream from sending their own patients to facilities they own; physician group practices and health entities would also face new ownership disclosure, billing identification, and compliance requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Physician-owned labs, imaging, and equipment firms

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves major self-referral channels intact: doctors could keep billing for in-office ancillary services furnished by their own employees, keep stakes in hospitals they practice at (if physicians own at least 60 percent), in ambulatory surgery centers, and in rural providers, so much of the conflict-of-interest problem would remain [S3].

The reporting, disclosure, and billing-identification requirements would impose ongoing paperwork and compliance costs on health entities and physician practices, which the CRS summary flags as government paperwork [S2].

Ownership exceptions and the Secretary's authority to add more exceptions by regulation create gray areas that physicians would have to navigate, and some legitimately capitalized arrangements would be swept up or require case-by-case rulings [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core problem the bill targeted was real: when doctors profit from the tests and services they order, patients and insurers can end up paying for care that may not be needed. The bill's remedy was broad but incomplete, keeping the large in-office ancillary channel open while banning outside self-dealing, and its compliance burden was substantial. A Congress that wanted to address self-referral could have done so at lower cost, and indeed later in 1993 enacted a much narrower version covering only laboratory services in the budget act.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote, it simply expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Bingaman introduced the bill on February 4, 1993, with Senator Howard Metzenbaum as the only cosponsor [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day of introduction [S5].
The bill's action history ends there: no hearing, no committee vote, no placement on a calendar, and no floor action ever occurred [S5].
Because the Congress ended on January 3, 1995, the bill died in committee without ever being voted on [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Physicians who owned stakes in labs, imaging centers, and equipment suppliers kept their referral income, and the health system continued paying for services ordered under those financial arrangements. Patients and payors saw no change, although Congress enacted a much narrower lab-only self-referral ban later in 1993 through the budget law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Physician-investors in labs and imaging centers

for.name: Sen. Jeff Bingaman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ethics in Referrals and Billing Act and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the Senate record shows it was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Metzenbaum.'

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the referral on February 4, 1993 — no hearing, no markup, and no vote to send the bill to the Senate floor.

against.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: As the committee's chairman during the 103rd Congress, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup, and it died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The only support on record came from two Senate Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote, so there is no record of how other members or either party would have voted.

industries.industry: Physician-owned labs, imaging centers, and medical equipment suppliers
industries.note: These businesses exist largely because doctors refer their own patients to facilities in which they hold a financial stake, and the bill would ban that referral income while barring collection on banned-referral claims. Patients and insurers would no longer foot bills generated by the doctor's own investment.

The bill would cut off outside self-referral income but carve out in-office ancillary services furnished by the physician or their employees, entrenching that in-office revenue channel. It also adds disclosure and billing-identification compliance work for group practices.
With referrals to physician-owned labs banned, independent labs would gain testing volume and would no longer compete against their own referrers' facilities.

Insurers could not be required to pay claims for services furnished through prohibited referrals and would gain disclosure of physician ownership, while the program could exclude violators from Medicare — reducing payments for potentially unnecessary ordered services.
